hook: The mass of one hydrogen atom is 0.000000000000000000000001674 g. Count those zeros twice and you may still get it wrong. Scientists write it as 1.674 × 10⁻²⁴ g instead: shorter, easier to compare, and easier to type into a calculator without slipping.

prereq.why: Multiplying powers of ten adds the exponents: 4 + (−7) = −3.
A negative exponent is a reciprocal: 1/10² = 1/100 = 0.01.

figure.caption: Scientific notation: a coefficient from 1 to just under 10, times a power of ten that says how many places the decimal point moved.

chain.cause: Very large and very small numbers carry many zeros
chain.effect: they are slow to write and easy to miscount

chain.cause: Any number can be split into a coefficient between 1 and 10 and a power of ten
chain.effect: the zeros move into the exponent

chain.cause: Moving the decimal point left makes the coefficient smaller
chain.effect: the exponent goes up by one for each place, so a large number gets a positive exponent

chain.cause: The exponent shows the size at a glance
chain.effect: comparing, multiplying and dividing become exponent arithmetic

ideas: Numbers above 10 get positive exponents; numbers below 1 get negative exponents.
Multiply: multiply coefficients, add exponents. Divide: divide coefficients, subtract exponents. Then fix the coefficient if it left the 1-10 range.
Add or subtract only after giving both numbers the same exponent. One order of magnitude is a factor of 10.

misconception.wrong: A larger coefficient always means a larger number, so 8 × 10⁻⁴ is bigger than 3 × 10⁻².
misconception.right: Compare the exponents first. 8 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.0008 and 3 × 10⁻² = 0.03, so the second is about 40 times larger. The coefficient only decides between numbers with the same exponent.

summary: Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient from 1 to just under 10 times a power of ten. Large numbers have positive exponents and small numbers negative ones. To multiply, multiply coefficients and add exponents; to divide, divide and subtract; to add, match exponents first. Each factor of ten is one order of magnitude.
